If there exists a god who helps during financial calamities or helps improve them (Such as Lakshmi in this religion), the devotee focuses his/her thought on such a form/force and prays in that direction.

This basically helps with teaching how to meditate and devote oneself. Having idols will help the devotee feel he/she has served the almighty for their aspirations. Most idols are symbolism, and all practices aid in visual support for the recitation of the vedas/mantra (Sorta like religious hymns) in situations to aid the devotee.

As one spends more time in devotion they may evolve to learn the forms of god are for focusing on worldly needs or desires, while the very same meditation learnt will help focus on a much higher goal, moksha (or unity with the bhraman/almighty). Sometimes it takes more than a few lifetimes to evolve from this phase.

Idolatory is a basic expression of spirituality - prayer to gods (visual forms) or demi-gods is for accomplishment of worldly goals. Weather it works or not is a matter of another debate. 

If you go a little historically, when vedic religion spread, it did not as such destroy religious practices of the locals, rather incorporated them at best. 

Even today, the gods prayed to (minor or less popular ones) would be different in the North of a country compared to south, yet the higher level spirituality or concepts of the same (The formless, omnipotent, etc god).

Maya: Worldly activities --> prayer with purposes (even world peace is a worldly purpose) --> accomplishment of the same --> prayer to gods attributed with qualities which will help one with the same -->may include meditating upon the said god.

Moksha:  Medidation in breaking free from the maya --> unity with the Bhraman.

TL;DR: Idolatory helps in the spiritual evolution where the devotee realizes, not just intellectually, that purpose of meditation or faith or whatever is unity with the bhraman.

1. Usually people don't care about the introduction - if you are the first to present, then you'll have to go through it all... if you are like the 7th person for the same professors, then you better keep it brief.

2. Talk about results for the most part - high light them as how you have got good information, while ascertaining the scientific process was pretty good. 

3. Keep conclusions brief (about 3~6 points) and then open the floor for questions.

4. Dumb fuck professors will ask questions on the methodologies - you can guess they did not understand much so you can answer them easily, confound them if you dont know well. Don't go too far though and get caught yourself.

5. Normal ones will ask you about interpretations of the results, how it will help and might ask you what you could have done and could not have - in this case - If it was a cheap/easy experiment suggestion, tell why that data would not fit in your thesis. if it was a costly expensive suggestion, say theses were initial results and it can be probed further based on funding and resources. Most times they'll suggest somthing that start discussing amongst themselves (the professors), just keep nodding and smiling.

6. The smart ones will challenge your premise and what could be the implications of your work. Answer the first part to the best of your knowledge while the 2nd part sparingly, leaving it open ended.

7. Its okay to say "I don't know" for 2/10 questions but only if it is something you did not perform.

For example: you cannot say "I dont know" when the question is, "Why did you perform this and this expt when you could have better quality of results using this experiment"

You can say "I don't know" when they ask knowledge based question like "what is the melting point of that one random chemical you used in just one time and is not too relevant in your study as your experiments never take it to that temperatures". Such dumbass questions are better avoided - as it might throw the floor open for more knowledge based questions.

8. Dessertations are made to push you to sweating point and to make you say "I dont knows" atleast a few times. Don't get too cocky nor look too stupid - pick and choose those "I don't knows" if possible, better if you can predict the next question based on your answer - sometimes they are designed to trap you.

9. Know the basics - the 80% of your questions will be on the basics. There's no point you explaining your new algorithm when you don't know what the If-then code exactly does in your program. 

10. When your guide steps in to defend you, better let him answer. But make sure you are talking for atleast 60% of the time for a good grade -else it'll seem like the guide is answering all the questions.
